title: Memory Care: The Signs It Is Time, What a Secure Unit Is, and How It Differs From Memory Support
description: When a parent with dementia needs memory care, what a secured unit in a Tennessee assisted living community is, what to look for, and what memory support means.
meta_title: Memory Care: When Is It Time, and What to Look For
meta_description: The signs a parent with dementia needs memory care, what a secured unit is, what to look for on a tour, and how it differs from memory support.
main_html:
Quick answer

It is time for memory care when dementia makes your parent unsafe, not when they are diagnosed. The clearest signs are wandering or trying to leave, getting lost in familiar places, being unable to stay alone safely, and distress or agitation that ordinary assisted living staff cannot manage. In Tennessee, memory care is a secured unit inside a licensed Assisted Care Living Facility; the state counts its beds as secured beds. Of the 31 licensed communities in Shelby County, 23 have them.

Memory care is a secured residential unit for people living with Alzheimer's disease or another dementia. The doors are locked or alarmed so residents cannot leave unnoticed, staff are trained in dementia care, and the day is structured to reduce confusion. In Tennessee these units operate inside licensed Assisted Care Living Facilities.

"Memory support" is not the same thing. Some communities use it for a programme of activities inside ordinary assisted living, with no secured unit behind it. That can be right for early dementia. It is not right for a parent who wanders.

The signs it is time

Look at the last three months, not the last good day. Families tend to measure against the good days; the risk lives in the bad ones.

  • Wandering or exit-seeking: leaving the house at night, trying doors, saying they need to "go home" while at home.
  • Getting lost: driving or walking somewhere familiar and not finding the way back.
  • Not safe alone: leaving the stove on, letting strangers in, missing or doubling medications, not eating.
  • Night-time confusion: sundowning, being awake and agitated at night, falls at night.
  • Behaviour others cannot manage: agitation, suspicion or aggression that overwhelms a spouse, family or assisted living staff.
  • Caregiver collapse: the person caring for your parent is exhausted, ill or no longer safe themselves.
  • Repeated calls from current staff: if your parent is in assisted living and the community keeps calling about wandering or behaviour, they are telling you something.

Any one of the first three is reason enough to look at memory care now.

Assisted living or memory care: a quick decision path

  1. Does your parent wander, try to leave, or get lost? If yes, memory care.
  2. Can your parent be left alone safely for an afternoon? If no, memory care is likely; ask a community to assess.
  3. Does your parent recognise when they need help and accept it from staff? If yes, assisted living with a memory programme may work for now.
  4. Is the dementia likely to progress quickly? If yes, choose a community with a secured unit on the same campus, so a later move is a short walk rather than a new community.

What a secured unit is

A secured unit is a part of the building, or a whole building, where residents cannot leave without staff knowing. Usually that means doors with keypads or alarms, an enclosed courtyard or garden, and no route out that bypasses staff. It is designed to let people with dementia move freely and safely, rather than be confined to a room.

A good secured unit also has:

  • A layout that is easy to understand: short corridors, a visible dining room, clear signs and memory cues on doors.
  • Safe outdoor space your parent can walk in whenever they want.
  • Calm lighting and noise levels; no constant overhead announcements.
  • Staff assigned to the unit, not borrowed from assisted living when they are free.
  • Activities planned around the residents' abilities and life histories, through the whole day, including the late afternoon when sundowning peaks.

The Tennessee Health Facilities Commission's bed report shows how many secured beds each licensed community has. In Shelby County they range from about fifteen in a small unit to communities where every licensed bed is secured. The directory on each city page shows the count.

"Memory support" versus memory care

SettingInside ordinary assisted livingA separate secured unit or building
DoorsOrdinary exitsLocked or alarmed, staff-controlled
StaffAssisted living staff, some dementia trainingStaff assigned to the unit and trained in dementia care
SuitsEarly dementia, no wandering, accepts helpWandering, getting lost, not safe alone, behaviour needing skilled response
State countNot counted as secured bedsCounted as secured beds

Ask any community that uses the phrase "memory support" whether it has secured beds on its licence. If it does not, it is not memory care.

What to look for on a memory care tour

  • Residents: are they engaged, calm, dressed and clean, or sitting in front of a television with nobody talking to them?
  • Staff: do they speak to residents at eye level, by name, calmly? Do they redirect gently rather than argue?
  • Staffing numbers: how many care staff are on the unit during the day, the evening and overnight? Ask for numbers, not "we staff to need".
  • Training: what dementia training do new staff get before working on the unit, and how often is it refreshed?
  • Turnover: how long has the unit's manager been there? How long have the care staff?
  • Medications: how are antipsychotic and sedating medicines used, and how often are they reviewed with the doctor?
  • Falls and wandering incidents: how are they recorded, and how is the family told?
  • Visit late afternoon. That is when sundowning is worst and staffing is often thinnest.

Our 40 tour questions include a full set for memory care.

Moving into memory care

Admission follows the same steps as assisted living: an assessment by the community's nurse, the physician's paperwork and medication list, and a residency agreement. Some differences:

  • The community will want to understand your parent's routines, history, likes and triggers. The more you tell them, the better the first weeks go. A one-page "about me" helps.
  • Agree how the move day will be handled. Many families find a calm, matter-of-fact move works better than long explanations.
  • Ask about visiting in the first weeks. Some communities suggest a short gap to let your parent settle; others prefer family close by. There is no single right answer; follow the staff's experience with your parent.
  • Bring familiar things: photos, a chair, a blanket, labelled clothes.

If your parent refuses or cannot understand the move, our guide on when a parent refuses to move covers how families handle it, including when a doctor or legal authority is involved.

What memory care costs

Memory care usually costs more than assisted living in the same community, because of staffing, training and the secured environment. It is often quoted as an all-inclusive rate. Compare all-in quotes, and ask how often the rate has risen. Medicare does not pay for memory care; TennCare CHOICES can pay for care services in an Assisted Care Living Facility, including its memory care unit, for people who qualify, but not room and board. See what assisted living costs and how families pay.

When memory care is no longer enough

As dementia advances, some residents need more than a memory care unit in assisted living can give: help with eating and swallowing, two-person transfers, complex medical care. Communities usually work with hospice for residents near the end of life, which can let a parent stay in a familiar place. Ask each community what would make it ask your parent to move to a nursing home, and how much notice it would give. The answer is in the residency agreement; our residency agreement guide explains where.

Questions to ask

  • How many secured beds do you have, and is one open now?
  • How many care staff are on the unit during the day, the evening and overnight?
  • What dementia training do staff complete before working on the unit?
  • How do you handle a resident who becomes agitated or tries to leave?
  • How do you involve the family in the care plan, and how often is it reviewed?
  • Do you work with hospice so residents can stay to the end of life?
  • What would make you ask my parent to leave memory care?

Getting a diagnosis and a care plan first

If your parent has not been formally assessed for dementia, ask their doctor for an assessment, or a referral to a memory clinic or neurologist. A diagnosis helps in three ways. It confirms what is causing the change, which may include treatable causes such as infections, medication side effects or thyroid problems. It gives the memory care community a medical picture to plan around. And it supports long-term care insurance claims and benefit applications.

The Alzheimer's Association runs a free round-the-clock helpline and has a chapter serving the Memphis area, with support groups and education for families. Caregivers who use these supports tend to make the move decision earlier and with less crisis.

Visiting a parent in memory care

  • Visit at the time of day your parent is at their best, often the morning.
  • Join an activity or a meal rather than sitting in the apartment.
  • Bring things to do together: photos, music they love, a simple task.
  • Do not quiz their memory. Enter their world rather than correcting it.
  • Keep goodbyes short and calm.
  • Get to know the care staff by name; they are your best source of how your parent really is.

The caregiver's health is part of the decision

Families often delay memory care because a spouse or adult child is still managing, at great cost to themselves. Caring for someone with dementia around the clock is exhausting, and caregivers' own health often declines: sleep loss, missed doctor's appointments, depression, injuries from helping with transfers. When the caregiver can no longer keep going safely, the person with dementia is no longer safe either.

It is reasonable to treat the caregiver's health as one of the signs it is time. Moving a parent into memory care does not end the family's role; it changes it from round-the-clock nursing to being a son, daughter or spouse again, visiting, advocating and spending time together without the constant tasks. Many families say that, looking back, they waited too long.

If you are not ready for a permanent move, adult day programmes and short respite stays in a memory care unit can give the caregiver regular breaks and let your parent get used to a new setting gradually.

faq.q: When is it time for memory care?
faq.a: When dementia makes your parent unsafe: wandering or trying to leave, getting lost in familiar places, not being safe alone, or behaviour that family or assisted living staff cannot manage. A diagnosis alone is not the trigger.

faq.q: What is a secured memory care unit?
faq.a: A part of a building, or a whole building, where doors are locked or alarmed so residents cannot leave without staff knowing. It usually has an enclosed garden and staff assigned to the unit and trained in dementia care.

faq.q: How many Memphis-area communities have memory care?
faq.a: The Tennessee Health Facilities Commission's July 2026 bed report shows 23 of the 31 licensed Assisted Care Living Facilities in Shelby County reporting secured memory care beds. Each city page lists them.

faq.q: Is memory support the same as memory care?
faq.a: No. Memory support usually means a programme of activities inside ordinary assisted living without a secured unit. Ask whether the community has secured beds on its licence; if not, it is not memory care.

faq.q: Can a parent with early dementia live in assisted living?
faq.a: Often yes, if they do not wander, can be left alone safely and accept help from staff. Choosing a community with a secured unit on the same campus avoids a second move to a new community later.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for memory care?
faq.a: No. Medicare does not pay for room, board or personal care in memory care. TennCare CHOICES can pay for care services for residents who qualify, but not room and board.

faq.q: What should I bring when my parent moves into memory care?
faq.a: Familiar things: photos, a favourite chair or blanket, and clothes labelled with their name. Bring a one-page summary of their routines, history, likes and triggers so staff can help them settle.

faq.q: Can my parent stay in memory care at the end of life?
faq.a: Many communities work with hospice so residents can stay. Ask what would make the community ask your parent to move to a nursing home, and how much notice it would give.
